purpose: Single source of truth for every load-bearing number, date and quotation in this project. Prose is authored per audience and may legitimately differ between a research note and a general-audience page. Values may not. Anything that renders a value reads it from here, and verify.sh section 6 asserts that each value still appears in the file named as its owner. If this file and the canonical file disagree, the harness fails and nothing ships.
vantage_note: Unless a fact says otherwise, it is asserted as of December 5, 1947, the date of Gödel's citizenship hearing. Powell v. McCormack (1969), the Twenty-fifth Amendment (1967) and modern state counts are out of bounds and must not be used to support any fact here.

status_values.verified: Checked against a primary source, and the check is reproducible.
status_values.unverified: Asserted from a secondary source or not yet checked. Renders with an explicit label.
status_values.disproved: This project claimed it and later refuted it. Kept visible on purpose.

facts.value: December 5, 1947
facts.label: Goedel's citizenship hearing
facts.statement: Kurt Goedel took his United States citizenship examination in Trenton, New Jersey, on December 5, 1947, with Einstein and Oskar Morgenstern as his witnesses.

source.title: Morgenstern memorandum, 'History of the Naturalization of Kurt Goedel'
source.note: Dictated September 13, 1971, twenty-four years after the events it describes.

facts.value: April 2, 1948
facts.label: Goedel swore the oath
facts.statement: Goedel was admitted to citizenship and swore the oath on April 2, 1948.

facts.value: September 13, 1971
facts.label: Date of the Morgenstern memo
facts.statement: The only surviving account of Goedel's claim is a memorandum Morgenstern dictated on September 13, 1971, opening with the admission that he was working from memory and had not checked his diaries.

facts.value: He rather excitedly told me that in looking at the Constitution, to his distress he had found some inner contradictions and that he could show how in a perfectly legal manner it would be possible for somebody to become a dictator and set up a Fascist regime, never intended by those who drew up the Constitution.
facts.label: The Morgenstern memo, on the claim
facts.statement: The sole first-hand description of what Goedel said he had found.

facts.value: he doubted Gödel was right
facts.label: The witness doubted the claim
facts.statement: The one witness to the claim recorded his own scepticism about it in the same document, and never says which part of the Constitution Gödel meant.

facts.label: Members of the House, 1947
facts.statement: The House of Representatives was fixed at 435 members by the Permanent Apportionment Act of 1929.

source.title: Permanent Apportionment Act of 1929
source.note: The statutory citation is recorded as ordinarily reported and has NOT been verified against Statutes at Large; the llsl retrieval problem in corpus/README.md is unsolved. The number 435 is not in doubt.

facts.label: Members of the Senate, 1947
facts.statement: Forty-eight states returned ninety-six senators.

facts.label: States in the Union, 1947
facts.statement: There were forty-eight states at the vantage date. Alaska and Hawaii were admitted in 1959 and are out of bounds.

facts.label: House quorum, 1947
facts.statement: A majority of the House, under Article I, Section 5, Clause 1.

facts.label: Senate quorum, 1947
facts.statement: A majority of the Senate, under Article I, Section 5, Clause 1.

facts.label: Representatives needed to propose an amendment
facts.statement: Two thirds of a House quorum, which is 33.6 per cent of the chamber, not the two thirds the text appears to require.
facts.checked_by: verify.sh section 2, where Z3 re-derives the figure by an independent route

source.title: National Prohibition Cases, 253 U.S. 350 (1920)
source.quotation: The two-thirds vote in each house which is required in proposing an amendment is a vote of two-thirds of the members present—assuming the presence of a quorum—and not a vote of two-thirds of the entire membership, present and absent.
source.read_from_note: Read from the page image rather than the OCR layer, which rendered both em dashes as hyphens.

facts.label: Senators needed to propose an amendment
facts.statement: Two thirds of a Senate quorum, which is 34.4 per cent of the chamber.

facts.label: Representatives, had the base been full membership
facts.statement: The figure the phrase 'two thirds of both Houses' is ordinarily taken to mean, and which the Supreme Court rejected in 1920.

facts.label: Senators, had the base been full membership
facts.statement: The counterfactual Senate figure on the rejected reading.

facts.label: States needed to ratify
facts.statement: Three fourths of forty-eight. This is where Article V's protection actually sits; the congressional gate is far weaker than the text suggests.

facts.label: State legislatures needed to compel a convention
facts.statement: Two thirds of forty-eight.

facts.value: Article V says two thirds of both Houses. It does not say two thirds of what.
facts.label: Article V does not state the base of its own fraction
facts.statement: Two thirds of the membership and two thirds of those voting are different numbers, and the text does not choose between them. Weimar Article 76 states its base explicitly; the same fraction appears in both documents and only one says what it divides.

facts.label: The case that fixed Article V's base
facts.statement: National Prohibition Cases, decided June 7, 1920, announced no conventional opinion but numbered conclusions. Conclusion 2 holds that the two-thirds vote Article V requires is two thirds of the members present, assuming a quorum, and not two thirds of the entire membership.

facts.value: Missouri Pacific Ry. Co. v. Kansas, 248 U.S. 276 (1919)
facts.label: Where Article V's base actually came from
facts.statement: The 1920 holding on Article V rests on a 1919 veto-clause case, which was itself justified in part by pointing at how Congress had long behaved under Article V. The base of Article V's fraction was never litigated on its own terms; it was ratified once by reference to what Congress had already been doing, and the doing came first.

facts.value: Taken end to end the American procedure is markedly more rigid, and the honest statement of this finding is narrow.
facts.label: The low congressional threshold does not make Article V weaker than Article 76
facts.statement: Weimar Article 76 was single-stage: four ninths of the Reichstag, with the Reichsrat, amended the constitution outright. Article V's congressional stage is lower, at about a third of each chamber, but it only proposes. Ratification by thirty-six of forty-eight state legislatures then had to follow, and Article 76 has no analogue to that. The comparison comes out the other way.
facts.guards_against: reading 146 as evidence that the United States was as exposed as Weimar

facts.value: Whatever protection Article V affords is carried almost entirely by the ratification stage, not by the supermajority in Congress.
facts.label: Where Article V's protection actually sits
facts.statement: This is the load-bearing sentence for later work, because it says where to look. A path that neutralises or bypasses state ratification faces a far weaker congressional threshold than the text implies.

facts.label: Rows in the 1947 silence inventory
facts.statement: Fields the Constitution does not reserve to itself, where ordinary legislation governs and no constitutional provision constrains what that legislation may say.

facts.value: Rows 4, 5 and 6 are the only entries a single chamber can alter with no concurrence from anyone
facts.label: Silences a single chamber can alter alone
facts.statement: No other chamber, no President, and on the 1947 law no court. These are the rows the quorum cascade chains together.

facts.value: Row 11 is the only entry where the silence has no filler at all
facts.label: The one silence with no filler at all
facts.statement: What 'Inability' means in Article II, Section 1, and who determines that it exists, was in 1947 settled by nothing: no statute, no rule, no decision. The Twenty-fifth Amendment was twenty years away.

facts.value: 328 U.S. 549, decided June 10, 1946, eighteen months
facts.label: The silence cluster is not ours
facts.statement: In Colegrove v. Green, decided eighteen months before the vantage date, Justice Rutledge concurring in the result named Article I sections 4, 2 and 5 as a group. The cluster was in the U.S. Reports before Gödel's hearing.

facts.label: Non-definitional axioms in the published model
facts.statement: Zahoransky and Benzmueller's Isabelle/HOL formalization of Goedel's claim carries fifty-one non-definitional axioms.

facts.label: Axioms that suffice for the dictatorship theorem
facts.statement: Dictatorship_t3 is provable from six of the fifty-one, and those six are consistent. Two are generic amendment-procedure rules, two are bare temporal-successor facts, and two stipulate that the dictatorship amendment is proposed and supported.

facts.label: Axioms necessary to every possible proof
facts.statement: Four of the six are necessary to every sufficient support, established by countermodels to the full theory minus each one. Six is irredundant but not proved minimum; the honest bound is 4 <= minimum <= 6.

facts.value: ⌊is_rat amd1a⌋t2
facts.label: What deleting Goedel's step one costs
facts.statement: Delete the four axioms proposing and supporting the amendment that strips Article V's entrenchment clause, and every published theorem and every intermediate lemma still proves, in a theory Nitpick confirms is still consistent. Two proof scripts break; both propositions are re-proved. What is lost is exactly one proposition: the ratification of the repeal itself, which the full theory entails and the reduced theory leaves independent.

facts.value: amd1a = (❙¬omsp)
facts.label: Why step one costs so little
facts.statement: The repealing amendment is extensionally equal to the negation of the entrenchment clause, provable without any of the model's non-definitional axioms. Its content is therefore already forced by the separate stipulation that the dictatorship amendment was proposed. The repeal's postcondition is available without the repeal. It is extensional equality, not a term identity: 'by (rule refl)' fails on this goal.

facts.label: Published theorems that survive the ablation
facts.statement: noDictatorship_t1, noDictatorship_t2 and Dictatorship_t3.

facts.label: Intermediate lemmas that survive the ablation
facts.statement: Three cite no amd1 axiom at all; the other two have proof scripts that name deleted axioms, and both propositions are re-proved without them.

facts.label: Independent witnesses collated for the Bill of Rights
facts.statement: The National Archives parchment transcription, the Senate rendering, GPO House Document 110-50, Cornell's Legal Information Institute, Yale's Avalon Project, and the Statutes at Large read from Library of Congress page scans.

facts.value: On wording the six agree completely.
facts.label: No divergence in word choice
facts.statement: Across all ten amendments there is not one divergence in word choice. Every difference found is orthographic or punctuational, which is precisely the class of difference this project cannot afford to normalize away.

facts.value: of the right of the people peaceably to assemble
facts.label: GPO corrupts the First Amendment
facts.statement: House Document 110-50 reads 'of the right' where the other five read 'or the right'. It is not trivial: 'or' makes assembly a fourth coordinate object of 'abridging', while 'of' subordinates it to 'the press'. Confirmed against a fresh download under two extraction modes, and located in body text rather than the index.

facts.value: Avalon deletes two commas
facts.label: Yale's Avalon Project drops two commas
facts.statement: The Fifth Amendment loses the comma before 'without just compensation' and the Seventh loses the comma after 'tried by a jury'. Cornell, which modernizes as aggressively in every other respect, keeps both. Avalon is alone among the six.

facts.value: at least three punctuations of the Second Amendment are in circulation across authoritative printings
facts.label: Punctuations of the Second Amendment
facts.statement: The Statutes at Large prints the Second Amendment twice and not identically, and both printings give one comma, which is neither the parchment's three nor the two of the widely circulated version.

source.title: Statutes at Large, volume 1
source.note: 1 Stat. 21 is the volume's front matter and reads a free State; 1 Stat. 97 is the Joint Resolution itself and reads a free state, lower case.

facts.history: An earlier version of corpus/README.md claimed the two-comma version appears in no source. That overreached: it was true of this corpus and false as a statement about the record. Corrected when the Statutes at Large was read directly.

facts.value: byte for byte in nine of ten amendments
facts.label: The Senate rendering reproduces the parchment
facts.statement: It diverges only by capitalizing 'Suits' in the Seventh, where GPO agrees with the Senate against the parchment. That makes it an independent confirmation of the parchment rather than a separate recension.

facts.value: For want of a comma, we have this case.
facts.label: O'Connor v. Oakhurst Dairy
facts.statement: A Maine dairy lost an overtime case in 2017 because of a missing comma, and settled the following year for five million dollars across 127 drivers. The opinion opens with this sentence.
facts.vantage_note: Modern, and cited as an illustration that punctuation carries legal weight. It is not evidence about 1947 and must not be presented as such.

facts.value: Every box was ticked. The rule was fine on its own terms and still authorized its own destruction.
facts.label: Germany, 1933 — collapse through the amendment clause
facts.statement: The Weimar constitution allowed amendment by a two-thirds vote. That vote was taken, and it changed the constitution into something that let one man make law.

facts.value: four ninths
facts.label: Weimar Article 76's two thirds composed to about 44 per cent
facts.statement: Article 76 required a two-thirds quorum and two thirds of those present. Those fractions compose. Two thirds of two thirds is four ninths, so the clause universally described as a two-thirds rule could be satisfied by about forty-four per cent of the statutory membership — less than half the chamber. It needs no source beyond the clause and multiplication.
facts.checked_by: arithmetic on the clause; no external authority required

facts.label: Votes for the Enabling Act, against 94
facts.statement: The usual telling is that excluding the 81 Communist deputies is what made the Act pass. The German Bundestag's later published account says the opposite: the majority would have sufficed for a constitutional amendment even had those deputies taken part. The exclusion was insurance, not the load-bearing element. An analysis resting on it rests on the wrong thing.

source.title: Deutscher Bundestag, on the Enabling Act of March 24, 1933
source.quotation: there would have been a sufficient majority for a constitutional amendment even if the Communist deputies had been able to take part in the vote

facts.value: a forgotten emergency economic law from 1917 that nobody had ever bothered to repeal
facts.label: Austria, 1933 — collapse through a statute outside the constitution
facts.statement: The government did not use the constitution at all. It reached outside it and governed through the 1917 act. If you were only reading the constitution, you would have seen nothing wrong. This is the case Gödel lived through.

facts.value: Not one of its eighty-four articles was amended.
facts.label: Italy, 1925 — collapse through ordinary law, text untouched
facts.statement: The constitution was never touched. Ordinary laws hollowed the state out around it, and a photograph of the document in 1848 and a photograph in 1925 look identical while everything real changed.

facts.value: A method that only reads constitutional text catches Germany and is blind to Austria and Italy.
facts.label: Why all three are kept
facts.statement: The three cases are a filter on this project's own methods, not a result. Any technique invented here has to rediscover all three before it is pointed at an open question.

facts.value: NOT A FINDING
facts.label: The quorum cascade is unverified
facts.statement: The cascade rests on the premise that the quorum base is 'members chosen and sworn' rather than the statutory chamber size. That premise has never been verified against pre-1947 authority. If the base is the statutory 435, the cascade collapses at step one.

facts.label: Checks in the verification harness
facts.statement: verify.sh re-runs every computational claim in the repository from scratch on a clean checkout. The number moves whenever a check is added, which is why it is asserted in exactly one place and the harness compares it against its own run.
facts.checked_by: verify.sh's own summary block, which fails if README.md advertises a different number

facts.label: Negative controls, designed to fail
facts.statement: Six checks assert something deliberately false that the tool must reject. A verification script that can only ever print PASS cannot distinguish a working toolchain from a broken assertion. Sections 2b, 2d, 3b, 4b, 4d and 6b.
facts.checked_by: verify.sh section 6d, which counts its own NEGATIVE CONTROL headers and compares them against the count stated in its header comment
facts.history: verify.sh's header comment said 'three' while five existed. The drift was found by tools/ssot_audit.py, not by the harness, because nothing was counting. Section 6d now counts.

facts.label: Loopholes found
facts.statement: No loophole has been found. The hypothesis is unproved and the search has not produced a candidate path through the Constitution. Everything in this repository that reads like progress is progress on the instruments.

facts.label: Claims made here and later disproved
facts.statement: Kept visible on purpose, because a repository that only records its wins is not evidence of anything.

facts.value: 219 where the hand derivation gives 218
facts.label: The solver answered a different question than the label claimed
facts.statement: A solver was asked for the minimum Representatives needed to pass an amendment and returned 219 where the hand derivation gives 218. The solver was right and the English label was wrong: it had been asked a subtly different question than the sentence written beside the answer. Nothing was broken, the output was correct, and no computer will ever catch that for you.

facts.value: three outcomes rather than two
facts.label: A timeout was reported as a refutation
facts.statement: The harness had a bug where a tool that ran out of time was reported as a tool that said no, producing a false inconsistency warning on about one run in six. The fix is a third outcome: PASS, FAIL, and INCONCLUSIVE for when a tool returns no answer at all. A search procedure that does not terminate is the normal case, and reporting it as a refutation manufactures findings.

facts.value: silently became inconsistent while still printing every theorem as proved
facts.label: A shipped experiment was vacuous
facts.statement: An ablation emitted axioms before the definition they mentioned, Isabelle generalized the free variable, and the reduced theory went inconsistent. An inconsistent theory proves every theorem you were hoping to see. Adversarial review caught it, not the harness. Every ablation now carries a mandatory consistency probe.
